prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We investigate the plasma flow properties inside a Supergranular (SG) cell, in particular its interaction with small scale magnetic field structures. The SG cell has been identified using the magnetic network (CaII wing brightness) as proxy, applying the Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to high spatial, spectral and temporal resolution observations obtained by IBIS. The full 3D velocity vector field for the SG has been reconstructed at two different photospheric heights. In order to strengthen our findings, we also computed the mean radial flow of the SG by means of cork tracing. We also studied the behaviour of the horizontal and Line of Sight plasma flow cospatial with cluster of bright CaII structures of magnetic origin to better understand the interaction between photospheric convection and small scale magnetic features. The SG cell we investigated seems to be organized with an almost radial flow from its centre to the border. The large scale divergence structure is probably created by a compact region of constant up-flow close to the cell centre. On the edge of the SG, isolated regions of strong convergent flow are nearby or cospatial with extended clusters of bright CaII wing features forming the knots of the magnetic network.

outputs.L1: We investigate the plasma-flow properties within a supergranular (SG) cell, with particular emphasis on its interaction with small-scale magnetic-field structures. The SG cell was identified using the magnetic network, traced by Ca II wing brightness, as a proxy and applying Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to high-spatial-, spectral-, and temporal-resolution observations obtained with IBIS. The full three-dimensional velocity-vector field of the SG cell was reconstructed at two distinct photospheric heights. To strengthen our findings, we also calculated the mean radial flow of the SG cell using cork tracing. In addition, we examined the behavior of the horizontal and line-of-sight plasma flows cospatial with clusters of bright Ca II structures of magnetic origin to better understand the interaction between photospheric convection and small-scale magnetic features. The SG cell investigated here appears to be characterized by an almost radial flow from its center toward its boundary. The large-scale divergence structure is likely generated by a compact region of persistent upflow near the cell center. At the edge of the SG cell, isolated regions of strong converging flow are located near or cospatial with extended clusters of bright Ca II wing features that form the knots of the magnetic network.
outputs.L2: We analyze plasma dynamics within a supergranular (SG) cell, focusing especially on how the flow interacts with small-scale magnetic structures. The cell was identified by using the magnetic network—traced through Ca II wing brightness—as a proxy and applying Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) to IBIS observations with high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution. We reconstructed the complete three-dimensional velocity field of the SG cell at two photospheric heights. To support these results, we independently derived the cell’s average radial flow through cork-tracing methods. We also examined horizontal and line-of-sight plasma motions coinciding with clusters of bright, magnetically generated Ca II features, seeking to clarify the relationship between photospheric convection and small-scale magnetic elements. The studied SG cell appears to exhibit a nearly radial flow directed from the center toward its boundary. Its large-scale divergent pattern is likely driven by a compact zone of persistent upflow near the cell center. At the SG perimeter, distinct areas of strong flow convergence lie close to, or overlap with, broad groupings of bright Ca II wing structures that constitute the magnetic-network knots.
outputs.L3:
A supergranular cell was identified in high-resolution observations obtained with the Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS). Brightness in the wings of the Ca II line was used as a proxy for the photospheric magnetic network, allowing the cell’s boundaries and evolution to be determined. The cell was then tracked using the Two-Level Structure Tracking technique, which provided measurements of the horizontal motions of intensity structures across the observed field.

By combining these horizontal velocities with line-of-sight Doppler measurements, the full three-dimensional plasma-velocity field was reconstructed at two photospheric heights. Cork-tracing experiments, in which passive numerical tracers were advected by the measured horizontal flow, were used to confirm the cell’s average radial-flow pattern. Particular attention was given to the horizontal and line-of-sight flows associated with clusters of bright Ca II structures driven by magnetic activity, providing insight into the interaction between convective motions and concentrated magnetic fields.

The reconstructed velocity field showed that plasma moved almost radially outward from the center of the supergranular cell toward its boundary. This organized outflow was likely sustained by a compact, persistent upflow region located near the cell center. At the cell’s edge, strong and highly localized convergent flows were detected. These convergence sites lay close to, or coincided with, extended clusters of enhanced Ca II brightness that form magnetic-network knots. The spatial association suggests that supergranular flows transport and concentrate magnetic flux at the cell boundary, where converging plasma motions contribute to the formation and maintenance of the magnetic network.
outputs.L4:
We investigated the dynamics of plasma flows and their interaction with small-scale magnetic structures inside a solar supergranular cell. The cell was identified from the enhanced brightness of the magnetic network observed in the wings of the Ca II line, which provided a clear outline of its boundaries. High-resolution spectroscopic observations obtained with the Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) were then analyzed using Two-Level Structure Tracking to determine the horizontal motions of photospheric intensity structures.

By combining the measured horizontal proper motions with line-of-sight Doppler velocities, we reconstructed the three-dimensional velocity field at two representative photospheric heights. This approach allowed us to compare the flow topology in different layers and to distinguish the dominant horizontal expansion from localized vertical motions. We also introduced passive tracers, or “corks,” into the measured velocity fields and followed their trajectories over time. The cork distributions provided an intuitive view of the transport produced by the flows and highlighted persistent convergence and divergence regions.

The resulting velocity maps revealed a largely radial, outward-directed flow throughout most of the supergranular interior. This organized expansion appeared to originate from a compact upflow near the center of the cell, consistent with the emergence of plasma that subsequently spreads horizontally through the photosphere. Although the overall pattern was coherent, the flow contained smaller-scale variations associated with granular and mesogranular motions. Differences between the two sampled heights further indicated that the flow geometry evolves with height rather than behaving as a strictly two-dimensional pattern.

At the periphery of the cell, the horizontal motions converged into several localized regions. Corks accumulated rapidly at these sites, showing that they act as effective sinks for material and embedded magnetic flux. The strongest convergence regions coincided with compact magnetic-network knots, demonstrating a close connection between the photospheric velocity field and the observed distribution of magnetic structures. These findings support a picture in which convection continually transports small-scale magnetic elements away from the supergranular interior and concentrates them at the cell boundary. The study therefore illustrates how the three-dimensional organization of photospheric flows contributes to the formation and maintenance of the solar magnetic network.
outputs.L5:
### The Supergranular Network in Ca II

The solar surface contains large convection cells known as **supergranules**, typically about 20,000–30,000 kilometers across. Plasma flows outward from the center of each supergranule and carries magnetic fields toward its boundaries. These boundaries form the supergranular network.

The network is especially visible in observations of ionized calcium, or **Ca II**, particularly the Ca II H and K spectral lines. Because these lines originate mainly in the Sun’s chromosphere, they reveal bright structures associated with concentrated magnetic fields. In Ca II images, the supergranular boundaries appear as a bright, web-like pattern surrounding darker cell interiors.

Studying the Ca II supergranular network helps astronomers investigate chromospheric heating, magnetic-field evolution, and the transport of energy through the solar atmosphere. It also provides insight into how small-scale magnetic activity contributes to the Sun’s larger and more dynamic behavior.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a solar physics paper investigating plasma flows within a supergranular cell and their interaction with small-scale magnetic structures using IBIS observations, Ca II wing brightness, Two-Level Structure Tracking, 3D velocity reconstruction, and cork tracing.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the three-dimensional plasma flow within a quiet-Sun supergranular cell and its interaction with small-scale magnetic structures using high-resolution observations from the Interferometric BIdimensional Spectrometer (IBIS). Horizontal proper motions are derived from Ca II wing-brightness images with the Two-Level Structure Tracking technique, while line-of-sight Doppler velocities are combined with the horizontal flow field to reconstruct the three-dimensional velocity topology. The resulting maps reveal a coherent large-scale outflow from the cell interior toward its boundaries, superposed on localized vortical and converging motions associated with granular and mesogranular evolution. Passive corks advected by the measured velocity field progressively accumulate in convergence lanes and at persistent flow sinks, where small magnetic elements are preferentially located and concentrated. The comparison between cork distributions, Ca II wing brightness, and magnetic features indicates that the supergranular flow organizes internetwork magnetic flux and transports it toward the network, while localized downdrafts and vortices contribute to flux aggregation and intermittently modify this transport. These results demonstrate the value of combining chromospheric-wing intensity tracking, Doppler measurements, three-dimensional flow reconstruction, and cork tracing to characterize the coupling between quiet-Sun convection and the evolution of small-scale magnetic fields.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study of the three-dimensional photospheric velocity field in a supergranule, emphasizing radial outflows, central upflows, convergent regions at the cell boundary, and their relationship to magnetic-network bright points.
counterfactuals.output:
The study reconstructs the three-dimensional photospheric flow in a supergranular cell by combining horizontal proper-motion measurements with line-of-sight Doppler velocities. The cell is dominated by a nearly radial horizontal outflow: plasma rises weakly near the center, spreads outward across the photosphere, and slows as it approaches the perimeter. The central upflow is broad and relatively weak, whereas the cell boundary contains narrow, stronger converging-flow regions, often accompanied by localized downflows.

Magnetic-network bright points are concentrated in these peripheral convergence zones. The horizontal motions advect small magnetic elements away from the cell interior and sweep them into intergranular lanes and supergranular boundaries, where converging and sinking plasma concentrates the magnetic flux. Thus, the observed network bright points trace the locations where the supergranular circulation terminates, rather than the central upflow or the divergent interior.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise scientific abstract explaining how high-resolution IBIS data and TST can be used to identify a supergranular cell, reconstruct plasma velocities at two photospheric heights, and analyze flows around clusters of bright Ca II magnetic features.
counterfactuals.output: High-resolution time-series observations from the Interferometric Bidimensional Spectrometer (IBIS) enable the dynamics of an individual supergranular cell to be mapped across the photosphere. The cell is identified from its coherent divergent horizontal-flow pattern and the concentration of Ca II brightenings along its network boundary. Two-Level Structure Tracking (TST) is applied to intensity structures sampled in spectral diagnostics formed at two photospheric heights, yielding horizontal proper-motion fields; Doppler shifts from the corresponding line profiles provide the line-of-sight component and permit reconstruction of the three-dimensional plasma velocity. Co-aligned Ca II intensity and magnetic maps are then used to locate clusters of bright magnetic features. Conditional velocity statistics around these clusters— including radial inflow, vertical motion, divergence, and vorticity—reveal how supergranular advection concentrates magnetic flux and modifies the surrounding plasma. This approach links height-dependent convection, network formation, and localized flows around magnetic elements at sub-arcsecond scales.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the methods and principal findings of an observational investigation into photospheric convection and small-scale magnetic fields inside a solar supergranular cell.
counterfactuals.output:
The investigation used a long, high-resolution time series of a quiet-Sun region near disk centre, chosen so that the field of view lay largely within one supergranular cell rather than on the strong magnetic network. Narrow-band spectropolarimetric images—typically supplemented by continuum intensity and Doppler measurements—provided:

- continuum maps of the granulation;
- line-of-sight velocities from spectral-line shifts;
- magnetic-flux maps from the circular-polarization signal, with full-Stokes inversions used where the signal permitted;
- horizontal proper motions obtained by local-correlation tracking of the granulation; and
- temporal tracking of individual magnetic patches to identify emergence, fragmentation, coalescence and cancellation.

Spatial and temporal averaging of the velocity field, together with “cork” or passive-tracer experiments, was used to reveal flow patterns larger and longer lived than individual granules.

### Principal findings

- **Convection was organized on several scales.** Ordinary granules evolved over minutes, but their collective motions formed persistent mesogranular-scale divergence centres and converging lanes within the larger supergranular circulation.
- **Internetwork magnetic flux was highly intermittent and mixed in polarity.** Most features were small, short-lived and weak, although some intensified to strong, nearly kilogauss concentrations after being compressed in intergranular downflows.
- **The fields were strongly controlled by convection.** New flux and horizontal fields were commonly detected in or near granular upflows. As the associated vertical footpoints developed, granular motions transported them into intergranular lanes.
- **Advection produced spatial organization.** Magnetic elements accumulated along mesogranular convergence lanes and especially at persistent flow sinks or lane junctions. Continued transport carried surviving flux toward the supergranular boundary and network.
- **Flux evolution was continuous.** Elements repeatedly split, merged, disappeared through cancellation with opposite polarity, or fell below the detection threshold. Thus the apparently diffuse internetwork field was maintained by a rapid cycle of emergence, transport, interaction and removal.
- **Mesogranular magnetic patterns need not represent a separate convection mode.** Much of the observed mesogranular organization could be explained by the correlated evolution of granules and by the long-term advection of magnetic tracers.

Overall, the study portrayed the interior of a supergranular cell not as magnetically empty, but as a continually renewed, mixed-polarity magnetic environment whose observable structure and evolution are largely dictated by photospheric convection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a research-paper abstract about measuring horizontal and line-of-sight flows in a supergranule, validating the mean radial flow through cork tracing, and finding central divergence with strong convergence near magnetic-network knots.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the plasma-flow structure of an individual solar supergranule by combining horizontal velocity estimates from local correlation tracking with line-of-sight Doppler measurements. The resulting flow maps reveal a predominantly radial, outward-directed motion across the cell interior, accompanied by systematic line-of-sight signatures consistent with the viewing geometry. To test the robustness of the inferred mean radial flow, we advect passive tracers (“corks”) through the measured horizontal velocity field. Their trajectories reproduce the expected transport from the supergranular center toward the boundary, independently confirming the azimuthally averaged radial-flow profile. Divergence maps show a broad region of positive divergence in the cell center, identifying the principal source of the horizontal outflow. In contrast, strong localized convergence occurs along the supergranular boundary, with the most intense sinks spatially associated with magnetic-network knots. Cork accumulation at these sites further demonstrates that the measured flow efficiently concentrates material and magnetic flux into the network. These results provide a coherent observational picture of supergranular circulation in which central divergent flows feed boundary-directed transport and terminate in compact converging regions associated with enhanced magnetic concentrations.
